{{Top|leg}}
{{Quote|In a specially fitted meteoroid, I traversed much of their region, making observations with less intrusive devices.|[[Osuno Whett]]|<ref name="Mindharp">''[[Lando Calrissian and the Mindharp of Sharu]]''</ref>}}
A '''meteoroid''' was an astronomical object.<ref name="Darksaber">[[Darksaber (novel)|''Darksaber'']]</ref> [[Osuno Whett/Legends|Osuno Whett]] once used a specially fitted meteoroid to travel across the [[ThonBoka|region]] of the [[Oswaft]] to observe the [[Species/Legends|species]] without being intrusive.<ref name="Mindharp" /> When [[New Republic/Legends|New Republic]] [[Warship/Legends|warships]] pursued the [[Darksaber (superweapon)|Darksaber]] [[Superweapon/Legends|superweapon]] through an [[Asteroid field/Legends|asteroid belt]], one of the [[CR90 corvette/Legends|Corellian corvettes]] was struck broadside by a large spinning meteoroid and fell behind in pursuit.<ref name="Darksaber" /> The [[Chol Nebula/Legends|Chol Nebula]] consisted of mostly [[Gas/Legends|gases]] but contained some bolder-sized meteoroids and dust clouds which were dense enough to prevent [[Sensor array/Legends|sensor arrays]] or [[Transmitter/Legends|transmitters]] penetrating the area, making it especially dangerous to navigate.<ref name="Beyond the Rim">''[[Beyond the Rim]]''</ref>

==Behind the scenes==
In real life, a meteoroid is a lump of rock or [[Iron/Legends|iron]] that [[Orbit/Legends|orbits]] around the sun.<ref name="National Geographic">{{WebCite|url=https://education.nationalgeographic.org/resource/meteoroid|text=Meteoroid|quote=Meteoroids are lumps of rock or iron that orbit the sun, just as planets, asteroids, and comets do.|work=[[Wikipedia:National Geographic|National Geographic]]|archivedate=20230519051742}}</ref> If it enters Earth's, or another [[Planet/Legends|planet's]], [[Atmosphere/Legends|atmosphere]] but burns up before it reaches the ground,<ref name="NASA">{{WebCite|url=https://solarsystem.nasa.gov/asteroids-comets-and-meteors/meteors-and-meteorites|text=What's the difference between a meteor, meteoroid, and meteorite?|quote='''Meteoroids''' are objects in space that range in size from dust grains to small asteroids. Think of them as "space rocks." When meteoroids enter Earth's atmosphere (or that of another planet, like Mars) at high speed and burn up, the fireballs or "shooting stars" are called '''meteors'''. When a meteoroid survives a trip through the atmosphere and hits the ground, it's called a '''meteorite'''.|work=[[Wikipedia:NASA|NASA]]|archivedate=20230423090620}}</ref> the streak of light that appears in the sky called a ''[[Meteor/Legends|meteor]]''.<ref name="Britannica What's">{{WebCite|url=https://www.britannica.com/science/meteor|text=What's the Difference Between a Meteoroid, a Meteor, and a Meteorite?|author=Gregersen, Erik|quote='''A meteor is the streak of light''' that you see in the sky when a small piece of cometary or asteroidal material enters the atmosphere at high speed and burns up because of the frictional heating from the piece's collision with the atoms and molecules in the atmosphere. '''Before the small bit of comet or asteroid enters Earth's atmosphere, it floats through interplanetary space and is called a''' '''''meteoroid.'''''|work=[[Wikipedia:Encyclopædia Britannica|''Encyclopædia Britannica'']]|archivedate=20230523235741}}</ref> A ''[[Meteorite/Legends|meteorite]]'', on the other hand, is a meteoroid that enters the planet's atmosphere and survives the trip and hits the ground.<ref name="NASA" /> Meteoroids range in size from tiny dust grains to about 330 [[Foot/Legends|feet]] (100 [[Meter/Legends|meters]]); space debris any bigger than this is considered an [[Asteroid/Legends|asteroid]].<ref name="HowStuffWorks">{{WebCite|url=https://science.howstuffworks.com/question486.htm|text=How big does a meteor have to be to make it to the ground?|quote=Meteoroids have a pretty big size range. They include any space debris bigger than a molecule and smaller than about 330 feet (100 meters) -- space debris bigger than this is considered an '''asteroid'''.|work=[[Wikipedia:HowStuffWorks|HowStuffWorks]]|archivedate=20230325103739}}</ref> Most meteoroids are fragments of asteroids and [[comet]]s, although a few are known to come from other planets and [[Moon/Legends|moons]].<ref name="Britannica and">{{WebCite|url=https://www.britannica.com/science/meteor|text=meteor and meteoroid|quote=Meteoroids are believed to be mostly fragments of asteroids and comets and are placed, with them, in the category of solar system objects known as small bodies. A few meteoroids also have come from the Moon, Mars, Vesta, and possibly Mercury.|work=[[Wikipedia:Encyclopædia Britannica|''Encyclopædia Britannica'']]|archivedate=20230307073411}}</ref>
